flashcards.q: What is clock skew?
flashcards.a: The difference between two machines' clock readings at the same moment.
flashcards.more: When NTP is healthy the difference is usually a few milliseconds, but never zero. If NTP is off or a VM has been paused, it can reach seconds or even minutes. So you can't make fine-grained decisions by comparing timestamps from two servers.

flashcards.q: What is clock drift?
flashcards.a: One clock slowly running ahead of or behind real time.
flashcards.more: A computer's clock counts the vibrations of a quartz crystal, and those change a little with temperature and age. Left uncorrected, a server can wander by several seconds a day. Drift builds up into skew between machines.

flashcards.q: What danger does NTP create for your code when it corrects a clock?
flashcards.a: The clock can suddenly jump forward or back, so the difference between two wall-clock readings can be wrong, even negative.
flashcards.more: For small errors NTP nudges the clock's speed up or down; this is called slew. For big errors it corrects in one jump, called a step. A backward step makes the same time occur twice, and code that assumed "time only moves forward" breaks.

flashcards.q: What is the difference between a wall clock and a monotonic clock?
flashcards.a: A wall clock tells the date and time and can jump. A monotonic clock only moves forward and measures how long something took.
flashcards.more: The wall clock is for showing people the time and stamping dates on records. The monotonic clock is the stopwatch: its reading is not a date, but the difference between two readings is always right. So use a monotonic clock for latency, timeouts and waits between retries.

flashcards.q: Which PHP function should you use to measure how long a task took?
flashcards.a: `hrtime(true)`: monotonic, with readings in nanoseconds. Not `time()` or `microtime()`.
flashcards.more: `time()`, `microtime()` and `new DateTimeImmutable()` all read the wall clock, so a difference between them is wrong when NTP corrects the clock. `hrtime(true)` never goes backwards. To get milliseconds, divide the difference by a million.

flashcards.q: What is a leap second, and what problem does it cause in code?
flashcards.a: An extra second occasionally added to UTC to keep it in step with the Earth's rotation. The same second can appear twice on a clock.
flashcards.more: The extra second is written as 23:59:60, but most systems can't represent that time, so they step back a second. This is exactly why negative time crashed Cloudflare's DNS on New Year 2017. The big clouds now spread the second over the whole day, which is called a leap smear.

flashcards.q: What is the right way to get the current time in Symfony?
flashcards.a: Inject `ClockInterface` and call `$clock->now()`, instead of calling `new DateTimeImmutable()` directly.
flashcards.more: Calling `new DateTimeImmutable()` directly ties the code tightly to the system clock, and you can't change time in tests. With `ClockInterface`, Symfony supplies the real clock in the app, and in tests you put in a `MockClock`.

flashcards.q: What is MockClock useful for?
flashcards.a: Freezing time in tests, and moving it forward with `sleep()` or `modify()` without really waiting.
flashcards.more: MockClock is a frozen clock: its time doesn't move unless you move it. So a rule like "expires after 30 days" can be tested in a few milliseconds, and the test gives the same result every run.

flashcards.q: Why can't you compare two servers' created_at values to say which event happened first?
flashcards.a: The two servers' clocks have skew. If the gap between the events is smaller than the skew, the timestamps can come out in the wrong order.
flashcards.more: For example, if A's clock is 80 ms ahead, an event on B 50 ms after one on A gets a smaller timestamp. To keep the order right you need a number issued by a single authority: a version or a sequence. More here: [[time/ordering-events/newer-edit-lost|Which came first?]]

flashcards.q: How do you get one agreed order for events written by several servers?
flashcards.a: Let one database number the rows (an identity column) and sort by that number. The price: one place hands out the numbers, and it is arrival order.
flashcards.more: `created_at` stays for display and reports. The `id` decides the order, because only one authority issues it. If you need the real order of changes to one entity, give the entity its own version number (see the ordering lesson).

flashcards.q: Why can't you order events from two machines by their clock timestamps?
flashcards.a: Every machine's clock differs (skew, drift, NTP jumps), so a larger timestamp doesn't mean it happened later.
flashcards.more: Two machines' clocks can differ by anything from a few milliseconds to several minutes. Even when one event caused the other, the timestamps can show the opposite order. So for cause-and-effect order you need something other than clocks.

flashcards.q: What is last-write-wins (LWW)?
flashcards.a: Of two changes, keeping the one with the larger timestamp and dropping the other. If clocks are wrong, the newer change is silently lost.
flashcards.more: It is simple, so many databases and sync systems use it. But a clock running ahead always wins, and the losing write disappears with no error. That is why it needs care.

flashcards.q: How does a Lamport clock work?
flashcards.a: Each machine keeps a counter. It goes up by 1 on every event, and on receiving a message it becomes max(own, received) + 1. The counter travels with messages.
flashcards.more: So anything known to have happened earlier always has a smaller number. For a total order, break ties on equal counters with the node id. It doesn't give real time; it only preserves cause-and-effect order.

flashcards.q: What is the limitation of a Lamport clock?
flashcards.a: If X happens before Y then counter(X) < counter(Y), but a smaller counter doesn't mean it happened first. Concurrent events can't be told apart.
flashcards.more: Two events with no message relationship between them are concurrent. Their counters can come out in either order. Detecting concurrency takes a vector clock, which uses more space.

flashcards.q: How do you keep order with version numbers?
flashcards.a: Increment `version = version + 1` atomically with each change. A consumer accepts only numbers higher than the one it knows and drops lower ones.
flashcards.more: On the database side, UPDATE … RETURNING version gives the order. On the consumer side, `UPDATE … WHERE version < :v`. Events arriving out of order still end up with the right result, because the smaller version is caught and dropped.

flashcards.q: Does a PostgreSQL sequence give COMMIT order?
flashcards.a: No. Sequence numbers rise in the order they are handed out. If a transaction with a larger number commits first, the smaller one can show up later.
flashcards.more: So reading events with a cursor like "I've read up to 100, now from 101" can miss some. Safe options: a per-entity version, or an outbox plus a separate progress marker.

flashcards.q: What is a hybrid logical clock (HLC)?
flashcards.a: A pair of clock time and a small counter: (time, counter). It reads like a clock and still preserves cause-and-effect order.
flashcards.more: If the clock goes backwards or stays equal, it bumps the counter to keep the order intact. Some multi-region databases use it internally. App developers usually don't have to build it.

flashcards.q: Do UUIDv7 or ULID give an exact event order?
flashcards.a: No. They sort by time, but across machines they depend on the clocks. The order is approximate, not proof of cause and effect.
flashcards.more: IDs created on one machine in the same millisecond are usually increasing. But if two servers' clocks differ, the order won't match. They are good for indexes, not for the true order of events.

flashcards.q: What is wrong with settling sync conflicts by the client's updatedAt?
flashcards.a: A client clock that is wrong or deliberately ahead always wins. And replacing the whole row loses other fields' changes.
flashcards.more: The client's time is never a basis for a decision. Detect conflicts with a server-assigned version, return 409 on a mismatch, and write only the fields that changed.

flashcards.q: Where should you store the time of a past event?
flashcards.a: In UTC, meaning PostgreSQL's timestamptz. Convert it to the user's zone when you display it.
flashcards.more: A past event (a payment, a login, an order) is one fixed moment. Stored in UTC, it stays the same moment wherever the server or the user is, and DST doesn't change it.

flashcards.q: How do you store a future local event, such as a meeting every Monday at 10 am?
flashcards.a: The local time (no zone) plus the zone name (Europe/London), and compute the UTC each time by that date's rules.
flashcards.more: Store only UTC and the meeting slides an hour when DST changes. Storing only "+01:00" doesn't help either, because the offset changes next season. The name gives you the right offset for every date.

flashcards.q: What is the difference between an offset and an IANA time zone?
flashcards.a: An offset (+01:00) is the UTC difference at one moment. An IANA zone (Europe/London) is all the rules for that place, DST included.
flashcards.more: London is +00:00 in winter and +01:00 in summer. Store "+01:00" and a winter meeting will be wrong. Store the zone name and tzdata works out the right offset, and if a government changes the rules, an update fixes it.

flashcards.q: What is a DST gap?
flashcards.a: When the clocks go forward in spring, one hour of local time doesn't exist. In London on March 29, 2026, 01:00-02:00 does not exist.
flashcards.more: If you try to place an event in that time, the code quietly moves it, in PHP to 02:30. Decide the rule: move to the next valid time, or tell the user.

flashcards.q: What is a DST overlap?
flashcards.a: When the clocks go back in autumn, one hour of local time happens twice. In London on October 25, 2026, 01:30 is two different moments.
flashcards.more: The local time becomes ambiguous. PHP picks one, and the user doesn't know which. Store UTC and the ambiguity disappears, because the two moments have different UTC times.

flashcards.q: How can PHP code tell whether a local time falls in a DST gap or overlap?
flashcards.a: Try the zone's offsets from the day before and after; keep each UTC moment that reads back as the same local time. Zero matches = gap, two = overlap.
flashcards.more: PHP won't tell you: it just shifts or picks. So list the real candidates yourself. With none, ask the user for another time. With two, choose earlier or later on purpose and store that UTC moment.

flashcards.q: What is the right way to compute "next week" for a weekly local event?
flashcards.a: Add `+1 week` in the local zone, then convert to UTC. Adding 168 hours in UTC shifts the time by an hour across DST.
flashcards.more: PHP's `DateTimeImmutable::modify('+1 week')` works in that object's zone, so the wall clock stays right. When the calculation is done, call `setTimezone(UTC)` and write the result to next_run_at.

flashcards.q: Why keep a next_run_at for a future local event with a scheduler?
flashcards.a: A scheduler compares only against UTC. Keeping the UTC computed from local time and zone in its own column makes the query simple and fast.
flashcards.more: `WHERE next_run_at <= now()` can use an index directly. After the event runs, the next date is computed again by the local rules and next_run_at is rewritten.

flashcards.q: What is the right format for sending a time from an API?
flashcards.a: ISO 8601 in UTC, ending in Z (for example 2026-04-06T09:00:00Z). Without Z or an offset, a browser assumes local time.
flashcards.more: Symfony's Serializer outputs DateTimeImmutable as RFC 3339 by default. Convert to UTC before exporting. In Vue, use `Intl.DateTimeFormat` with `timeZone` to show it in the user's zone.

flashcards.q: How do you get the user's browser time zone in Vue?
flashcards.a: `Intl.DateTimeFormat().resolvedOptions().timeZone` (for example America/New_York). Pass it as the `timeZone` option of `Intl.DateTimeFormat` to format times.
flashcards.more: Intl follows DST rules itself, so you never add or subtract hours by hand. For an event in another city, also show the time in the event's zone, so nobody gets confused.

flashcards.q: Whose clock should decide expiry?
flashcards.a: The server's. A client's clock can be wrong or deliberately changed, so it can't be used for a security decision.
flashcards.more: The client only displays the remaining time the server gave it. On every request the server checks expiry against its own Clock. That way nobody can extend a trial or an OTP by changing the phone's date.

flashcards.q: What is the difference between a deadline and a duration?
flashcards.a: A deadline is a fixed moment (invalid after 10:05 UTC). A duration is a length of time (300 seconds).
flashcards.more: A deadline is better for storing expiry, because everyone sees the same moment. For counting down or measuring a wait, a duration and a monotonic timer are right. The usual rule: turn the ttl into expires_at when you issue, and store that.

flashcards.q: What is a monotonic clock, and why is it good for measuring timeouts?
flashcards.a: A clock that never goes backwards. It doesn't jump when NTP or a person changes the time, so it is safe for measuring how much time has passed.
flashcards.more: In PHP it is `hrtime(true)`, in the browser `performance.now()`. They don't tell the date; they only say how far time has advanced. The wall clock (`time()`, `Date.now()`) is good for knowing the date, not for measuring a length.

flashcards.q: What should the server send to show a countdown to a client?
flashcards.a: The seconds remaining (say 297). The client counts it down with a monotonic timer, and the phone's date isn't needed.
flashcards.more: Send expires_at and the client compares it with its own clock, giving a wrong countdown if that clock is wrong. Send the remaining time and the client's clock drops out. The final decision is still always the server's.

flashcards.q: What is a grace period, and how big should it be?
flashcards.a: A little extra time after expiry, to cover network delay and slight clock differences. In security, a few seconds, no more.
flashcards.more: In JWT it is called leeway (usually 5-30 seconds). Business grace is different: keeping the service on for 3 days after a subscription ends. Keep the two apart in name and in code, or they get mixed up.

flashcards.q: What is a timeout budget?
flashcards.a: One total time limit for the whole request, divided among the steps. Each step gets only what remains.
flashcards.more: If the client waits 3 seconds, all the inner calls together must take less than 3 seconds. A `Deadline` object counts with hrtime and, once the budget is spent, throws an error instead of starting new work.

flashcards.q: What are `timeout` and `max_duration` in Symfony HttpClient?
flashcards.a: `timeout` is the idle timeout (waiting when no data arrives). `max_duration` is the total limit for the whole request, in seconds; 0 or less means unlimited.
flashcards.more: A server that trickles data slowly doesn't trip the idle timeout, but it does trip max_duration. To hold a budget you need max_duration. And when the budget is spent, don't pass 0, because 0 means unlimited.

flashcards.q: What happens when an inner timeout is bigger than the outer timeout?
flashcards.a: The outer client gives up, but the work inside carries on. If it ends up succeeding, the user never learns of it.
flashcards.more: The rule: all the inner timeouts (retries included) must add up to less than the outer timeout. Otherwise the server burns resources for nothing, and the outcome goes around as "unknown".

flashcards.q: How do retries affect a timeout?
flashcards.a: They multiply the worst-case total: (retries + 1) × timeout per attempt + delays. Work it out first and keep it inside the budget.
flashcards.more: 3 retries means 4 attempts × 10 seconds = 40 seconds, while the client is on 3. Reduce the attempts and shorten each attempt's limit. And if you must retry a call that charges money, you need an idempotency key.

flashcards.q: What happens to your PHP workers when an outbound call has no timeout?
flashcards.a: Each worker that calls the hung service waits. Once all workers are stuck, the site stops answering. Set `timeout` and `max_duration` on every call.
flashcards.more: A PHP-FPM pool has a fixed number of workers, say 20. If a gateway hangs, 20 requests that touch it are enough to occupy them all, and even pages that never call the gateway stop loading. A budget-sized max_duration turns "hang" into a fast error.
